title: Checkpoint: The Varṇamāla
summary: A cumulative examination of the whole alphabet: the sixteen vowels, the twenty-five letters of the varga grid, the eleven outside it, and the two marks counted with neither. Twenty-eight questions in the four examination formats.

drills.stem: How many అచ్చులు does the traditional varṇamāla count?
drills.explanation: Sixteen vowels, against thirty-six consonants — fifty-two letters in all.

drills.stem: Which letter is **ఈ**?
drills.explanation: ఈ is long ī. Short i is ఇ, and the two differ by a loop — one of the pairs that must be told apart at speed.

drills.stem: Which letter is the **long** partner of ఒ?
drills.explanation: ఒ pairs with ఓ. ఔ is the diphthong au, which closes the o-group but is nobody's length-partner.

drills.stem: Which of these letters are **diphthongs**?
drills.explanation: ఐ and ఔ are the two diphthongs and have no short partner. ఏ and ఊ are long vowels, which is a different thing entirely.

drills.stem: What is the **తలకట్టు**, and why does it matter?
options: A mark of vowel length; it matters because length distinguishes words.
The headstroke forming part of most letters; it matters because a subjoined consonant loses it.
A punctuation mark; it matters because it ends a sentence.
The mark that mutes the inherent vowel.
drills.explanation: It carries no meaning of its own — it is part of the letter's shape. Its importance is negative: losing it is what makes subjoined forms hard to recognise.

drills.stem: When is an **independent** vowel letter such as ఇ written?
options: Only where the vowel is not preceded by a consonant.
Only at the end of a word.
Only where the vowel is long.
drills.explanation: After a consonant a vowel is written as an attached sign instead. ఇల్లు begins with a vowel and so is written with ఇ; తెలుగు begins with a consonant and so is not.

drills.stem: Telugu has separate letters for short **e** and short **o**. What does that tell you about the language?
options: That it borrowed its script from Latin.
That it is Dravidian, and needs letters for sounds Sanskrit has not got.
That its vowels are all long.
drills.explanation: Sanskrit has no short e or o; the southern languages do, and their scripts had to provide for it. Keeping ఎ and ఏ apart is a mark of a Dravidian script.

drills.stem: How does Telugu sound the letter **ఋ**?
options: as a bare r with no vowel
drills.explanation: ఋ is a vocalic r inherited from Sanskrit. Hindi sounds it *ri* and Telugu *ru* — ఋషి is *rushi*. It is the only one of the four vocalic letters a modern reader meets.

drills.stem: Of the sixteen vowels, how many would a reader of modern Telugu actually meet in print?
drills.explanation: Thirteen: the ten of the five short–long pairs, the two diphthongs, and ఋ. ౠ, ఌ and ౡ are dead letters that the traditional list keeps out of respect for Sanskrit.

drills.stem: What sound does the letter **మ** stand for?
drills.explanation: *ma*. Every consonant letter carries the vowel అ inside it — that is what makes the script an abugida and not an alphabet.

drills.stem: Which letter is **న** (na)?
drills.explanation: న is the dental nasal. ణ is the retroflex nasal, ఞ the palatal, మ the labial — four of the five nasals, and telling them apart is much of the work of the grid.

drills.stem: Which letter is the **nasal** of the velar varga?
drills.explanation: ఙ, fifth of the ka-varga — the ng of "sing". It is rarely written, the anusvāra doing its work, but it is a letter of the alphabet all the same.

drills.stem: Which letter is the **voiced aspirate** of the dental varga?
drills.explanation: Fourth in the varga is always the voiced aspirate, giving ధ. త is unvoiced, థ unvoiced aspirated, ద voiced but unaspirated.

drills.stem: Which of these letters are **retroflex**?
drills.explanation: ట, డ and ణ belong to the retroflex varga. త is its dental counterpart — the pair English speakers hear as one sound and Telugu keeps rigidly apart.

drills.stem: What do **గ, జ, డ, ద, బ** have in common?
options: They are made at the same place in the mouth.
They are all third in their varga — voiced and unaspirated.
drills.explanation: They share a column, one from each varga: voiced, unaspirated, differing only in place. Sharing a place would mean sharing a varga, and they come from five different ones.

drills.stem: **తలుపు** is written with three consonant letters and one vowel sign. Setting the sign aside, how many sounds do the three letters alone stand for?
drills.explanation: Six: each consonant letter carries its own vowel, so three letters give three consonants and three vowels. Counting three is the error of a reader trained on an alphabet, where a letter is one sound.

drills.stem: How many హల్లులు does the traditional varṇamāla count?
drills.explanation: Thirty-six: twenty-five in the vargas and eleven outside them.

drills.stem: Which letter is **వ** (va)?
drills.explanation: వ is the semivowel sounded between English v and w. య, ర and ల are the other three అంతస్థాలు.

drills.stem: Which sibilant is **palatal** — the ordinary *sh*?
drills.explanation: శ is palatal, ష retroflex, స dental. The three differ only in place, exactly as the vargas do, and an English ear hears the first two as one sound.

drills.stem: What is unusual about **క్ష**, the thirty-sixth letter?
options: It is a vowel listed among the consonants.
It is not a simple sound but the conjunct of క and ష.
It is written only at the end of a word.
drills.explanation: It is two consonants written together, admitted to the alphabet by tradition. Its inherent vowel it carries like any other consonant.

drills.stem: Which of these letters are made with the tongue **curled back**?
drills.explanation: ష is the retroflex sibilant and ళ the retroflex lateral. స and ల are their plain counterparts. The retroflex series runs through the whole alphabet, inside the vargas and outside them alike.

drills.stem: The same mark ం is sounded *ṇ* in పండు and *m* in పుస్తకం. Why?
options: Because ం is silent and the reader supplies a sound.
Because the anusvāra has no place of its own: it takes the nasal of the varga after it, and is m at the end of a word.
Because ం is a vowel whose length varies.
drills.explanation: One mark, five possible sounds. డ is retroflex, so ం is ṇ; at the end of a word there is nothing following to borrow from, and it is sounded m.

drills.stem: Which statements about ం and ః are correct?
options: They are counted among the sixteen vowels.
Each is a mark written upon a vowel rather than a letter of its own.
Leaving them out of the count is why the alphabet totals fifty-two.
drills.explanation: They are counted with neither vowels nor consonants — hence 'of both kinds'. Counting them in would give fifty-four.

drills.stem: What has become of **ఱ** in modern Telugu?
options: It is the commonest letter in the script.
It is obsolete, and ర is written in its place.
It is written only before a nasal.
drills.explanation: *Baṇḍi ra* was once a separate trilled r and is now dead. The traditional count of thirty-six keeps it, which is why the taught alphabet and the working one differ.

drills.stem: Which letter is **ళ**?
drills.explanation: ళ is a retroflex lateral — a Dravidian sound absent from Sanskrit, and very common in Telugu: నీళ్ళు, water, contains two.

drills.title: A page from the varṇamāla
drills.passage:
క ఖ గ ఘ ఙ
చ ఛ జ ఝ ఞ
ట ఠ డ ఢ ణ
త థ ద ధ న
ప ఫ బ భ మ
drills.translation: The varga grid: velar, palatal, retroflex, dental and labial, each row running unvoiced, unvoiced aspirated, voiced, voiced aspirated, nasal.

questions.stem: Which letter stands in the **last column of the third row**?
questions.explanation: The third row is the retroflex varga and the last column the nasal, giving ణ. న is the dental nasal in the row below.

questions.stem: Reading the chart, which statements are correct?
options: The second and fourth columns hold the aspirates.
The rows run from the front of the mouth to the back.
The letters of one column share a manner of articulation.
questions.explanation: The rows run **back to front** — velar, palatal, retroflex, dental, labial — not front to back. Everything else the chart shows plainly once the two axes are understood.

questions.stem: Reading down the **fourth column** of the chart, how many of those letters are voiced?
questions.explanation: All five. The fourth column is the voiced aspirates — ఘ ఝ ఢ ధ భ — so voicing is what the whole column has in common, and the count is the height of the chart. A reader who checks each letter separately gets the same answer more slowly.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985.
